title: SteelSeries Rival Pro ve Sensei Pro tanıtıldı: UWB ve değiştirilebilir batarya
summary: SteelSeries, UWB bağlantı teknolojisi, 53 gram ağırlık ve sıcak değiştirilebilir batarya sistemine sahip yeni Rival Pro ve Sensei Pro kablosuz oyuncu farelerini duyurdu.
body:
SteelSeries, oyuncu ekipmanları pazarındaki iddiasını yenilemek amacıyla **SteelSeries Rival Pro** ve simetrik kardeşi Sensei Pro modellerini 29 Eylül'de duyurdu. Ergonomik tasarımı ve hafifliğiyle dikkat çeken yeni kablosuz oyuncu fareleri, 13 Ekim'de 179,99 dolar fiyat etiketiyle raflardaki yerini alacak.

## Öne çıkan teknik özellikler ve UWB bağlantı

Yeni fareler, standart kablosuz aksesuarlarda kullanılan 2.4GHz frekansı yerine 6.4GHz ile 9.056GHz arasındaki ultra geniş bant (UWB) teknolojisini kullanıyor. Bu sayede kalabalık sinyal kirliliğinden kaçınan cihazlar, daha yüksek bant genişliği ve düşük gecikme vadediyor. Siyah ve beyaz renk seçeneklerinde 53 gram ağırlığa sahip olan modeller, 42.000 DPI hassasiyet sunuyor. Ayrıca seride, dört gram daha hafif olan mini versiyonlar da yer alıyor.

## Değiştirilebilir batarya ve yazılım desteği

Cihazlar, kablo bağlantısı için hiçbir USB portuna yer vermezken, şarj istasyonunda yedek tutulabilen dairesel sıcak değiştirilebilir batarya sistemiyle geliyor. 8.000Hz tarama hızında her bir batarya 16 saat kullanım sunarken, bu oran 1.000Hz'e düşürüldüğünde 60 saate çıkıyor. Yanında gelen GG uygulaması ve tarayıcı tabanlı web desteği, SuperSync ve Smart DPI gibi özelliklerle özelleştirme imkânı tanıyor.

**Neden önemli?** SteelSeries'in yeni serisi, 2.4GHz tıkanıklığını aşmak için UWB bağlantısını ve kesintisiz kullanım için değiştirilebilir batarya sistemini bir araya getirerek rekabetçi e-spor pazarında yenilikçi bir alternatif sunuyor.

source_texts.title: SteelSeries’ new mice are super light, have UWB and swappable batteries
source_texts.summary: The new ergonomic Rival Pro and ambidextrous Sensei Pro wireless gaming mice are some of the company's most interesting models in years. They're familiar designs that feel incredibly lightweight to hold (53 grams each in black, one gram more in white), and they ship with two signature SteelSeries features found in its other product categories: […]
source_texts.text:
The new ergonomic Rival Pro and ambidextrous Sensei Pro wireless gaming mice are some of the company’s most interesting models in years. They’re familiar designs that feel incredibly lightweight to hold (53 grams each in black, one gram more in white), and they ship with two signature SteelSeries features found in its other product categories: swappable batteries and a wireless base station to pair to.
SteelSeries’ new mice are super light, have UWB and swappable batteries
The Rival Pro and Sensei Pro (and their mini counterparts) launch October 13th for $179.99 each.
The circular batteries are easy to use, unlocking and locking in place in the mouse and base station. The station can keep a spare charged — and you might need it sooner than you think, as each battery is rated to last for 16 hours in the 8,000Hz polling rate. I’ve swapped these batteries at least six times during my few weeks of testing, though knocking the polling rate down to 1,000Hz boosts it to 60 hours for each battery.
Instead of using 2.4GHz like most wireless gaming accessories, these mice communicate with their base station via ultra-wideband (UWB) between 6.4GHz and 9.056GHz, giving them access to parts of the spectrum that aren’t cluttered by signals from any (or, at least, as many) nearby consumer electronics. SteelSeries says that this affords the mice 20 times the bandwidth and lower latency, and it’s used to deliver high polling rates with better consistency than other brands.
The mice launch alongside some new developments for the GG companion app. There’s SuperSync, a feature that decouples click and sensor polling, letting you have, say, 8,000Hz click reporting and 4,000Hz sensor reporting. SteelSeries says that decoupling them should lessen the burden on your CPU with 8,000Hz enabled, and may work better in games that have incompatibility issues with high polling rates. There’s also Smart DPI, a feature that can automatically adjust DPI when transitioning from in-game to navigating through menus, slowing when it comes time to make a selection in a menu, and returning to your preferred sensitivity when you resume the game.
One of my favorite new updates is that GG is available as a browser-based web app now in Chrome or Edge, not just as something you need to download. The feature-reduced web version seems good in a pinch, letting you install firmware updates and adjusting simple settings. It’s always nice to see more gaming companies adopt web-based alternatives.
The Rival Pro and Sensei Pro cost $179 each and are available to preorder now, shopping on October 13th. SteelSeries is also releasing miniature versions of both form factors that weigh four grams less and cost the same price.
I’ve been expecting more gaming companies to take on Logitech’s X2 and X3 Superstrike with haptics-based mice of their own. Perhaps those will come someday, but swappable batteries and better connectivity via UWB prove that there are still plenty of appealing ways to improve on mice before moving on from mechanical switches.

source_texts.title: SteelSeries just re-entered the chat: I spent a month testing its new elite gaming mice
source_texts.summary: Could ultra-wideband be the future of gaming mice? I tested the SteelSeries Rival Pro to find out.
source_texts.text:
Tom's Guide Verdict
SteelSeries just re-entered the chat with the Rival Pro. This esports mouse packs performance and responsiveness, utilizing 6GHz UWB connectivity for the most accurate tracking around. There’s a zero downtime battery system and loads of customization potential via the GG standalone and web apps. My only major issue is that you’ll get more click features via analog switches elsewhere, if that’s your thing, and that the black version is a total fingerprint magnet.
Pros
- +Lightweight and responsive
- +6GHz UWB connectivity
- +8K sensor and click polling
- +Zero downtime battery
- +Customizable via GG
Cons
- -Optical switches kinda boring
- -Fingerprint magnet
Why you can trust Tom's Guide
The time has come for SteelSeries to get back into the elite mouse game. While the brand has been pumping out the odd mouse here or there, it knows it’s been falling a little behind its rivals when it comes to cutting edge competition mice. Enter the new SteelSeries Rival Pro and its symmetrical sibling, the Sensei Pro — the latter named, of course, after SteelSeries’ legendary Sensei mouse from 2011.
The Rival and Sensei pack some powerful specs and interesting features, including Ultra-wideband (UWB) connectivity through to 8K oversampled polling, 8K reporting and 42,000 DPI sensitivity. There’s also zero downtime battery life (SteelSeries’ favorite thing these days), plenty of customization via the GG app and, in a first for SteelSeries, web app support.
So could this be one of the best gaming mice for esports and competitive players. Read my full SteelSeries Rival Pro review to find out.
Note, this mouse is available in either ergonomic (Rival) or symmetrical (Sensei) profiles, and in two sizes (Pro being larger, Mini smaller). I’ve covered the Rival Pro here because I spent the most time with it gaming at home (I prefer a larger ergo mouse). But I've also used the Sensei Pro for all test gaming at work. Internally, they're all the same.
SteelSeries Rival Pro review: Cheat sheet
- What is it? A competition gaming mouse from SteelSeries
- Who is it for? Elite or highly competitive players
- What does it cost? $179 / £169
- What do we like? The UWB connectivity, zero downtime battery, responsive performance, and high levels of customization
- What don’t we like? The black model is a fingerprint magnet, and its optical sensors feel a little featureless versus competition
SteelSeries Rival Pro review: Specs
SteelSeries Rival Pro review: The ups
The SteelSeries Rival Pro is an elite gaming mouse through-and-through. It offers bags of performance and stability, low weight, and plenty of customization.
Ultra-wide band connectivity
Key to the Rival Pro’s performance is its connectivity. Instead of the usual 2.4GHz connectivity we typically see on mice, the Rival uses Ultra-wideband (UWB), which operates in the 6GHz band instead of 2.4GHz. Why? Because everything else you’re running over 2.4GHz can cause connection dropouts for the others.
As some of your devices hog 2.4GHz channels, there can be a momentary pause while other devices hunt for a free channel. On most tech, this doesn’t matter — that hunting takes milliseconds. But on a mouse, which has to track so quickly and accurately, and across so many pixels, those millisecond hunting dropouts can leave you with dead zones in cursor coverage. What happens if an enemy’s head is in that dead zone? No headshot, that’s what. And you’re probably dead as a result.
By using UWB, which has more bandwidth and less other stuff on it, the Rival Pro ensures no dead zones and better tracking accuracy. Your cursor should be wherever you actually put it, every time. All the main competition — the Logitech G Pro X Superlight 2 ($159) and Pro X3 SuperStrike ($199), the Razer Viper V4 Pro ($159) and the Corsair Sabre V2 Pro ($99) — use 2.4GHz.

The downside of UWB is its connectivity range, which is very short, but enough to cover a mousemat area on your desk. That short connectivity range also means other UWB tech likely isn’t going to interfere unless you have them right next to one another. And even then, it won’t be an issue. Let’s say you put an UWB AirTag on your desk within your Rival Pro’s connectivity bubble: UWB covers 6GHz to 9GHz, meaning there’s lots of space and bandwidth to avoid crossovers, and most UWB devices use a very narrow channel within that wider range anyway.
The main UWB hub and charging dock are obviously not ideal for carrying around. Thankfully, SteelSeries also makes a USB-C travel dongle, although it's a separate $24 purchase.
Lightweight and responsive

CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7700X | Graphics card: MSI RTX 5070 Ti 16GB Vanguard SOC | Motherboard: MSI B850E Gaming Plus WiFi | RAM: Kingston Fury Renegade DDR5 32GB | Cooler: Noctua NH-U12S | PSU: MSI MEG Ai1300P PCIE5 | Case: MSI MPG GUNGNIR 110R
As SteelSeries puts it: if you suck already, the UWB stuff and ultra high poll rates won’t magically turn you into a competitive FPS player. However, the Rival Pro’s inherent lightness and responsiveness will definitely help up your game regardless of existing skill.
While I’m no esports player at Counter-Strike 2, I don’t suck, and I definitely felt the benefit of the Rival Pro’s rapid sensor and streamlined design. With up to 42,000DPI and up to 70G of acceleration, you can zip your cursor across the screen with just a tiny flick. But you can also customize the acceleration profile in the GG app to get it just right for you. There are several behavior profiles (linear, etc) to get you started.
The Rival Pro is also super lightweight at 53g for the Rival and Sensei Pro, and 49g for the Mini variants. That makes it effortless to slide rapidly across your desk, feeling extremely snappy and responsive. I felt I was able to move and turn quicker and more accurately in Wardogs and Counter-Strike, helping me score kills when reacting to stuff going on behind me. I also played Hell Let Loose and Isonzo with much the same benefits. I had a lot of trouble going back to my heavy Logitech MX Master 4 ($119) after using the Rival Pro.
The 53g Rival/Sensei are lighter than the Logitech G Pro X Superlight 2 at 60g (51g for the mini variant) and the X2 SuperStrike ($179) and X3 SuperStrike, each weighing 61g. The Razer Viper V4 Pro and Fnatic x Lamzu Maya 8K ($119) weigh less, though, at 49g and 44g.
Oversampled 8K polling
Set at the highest poll and sensor report rates of 8K, movement feels incredibly smooth, too. Fun fact: the 8,000Hz polling is actually oversampled down from 9,000Hz — an extra ninth data package is sent after every eighth, providing extra redundancy against instability. Mostly theoretical, of course, as you’ll never actually notice this, but nice to know.

source_texts.text:
Our Verdict
SteelSeries has finally returned to top form in the top-tier competitive gaming mice niche. Given its ergonomic shape, the Rival Pro will only be for those who like to use a palm grip, but for such gamers, you can't ask for much more. It's comfy, well-built, satisfying to use, and has hot-swappable batteries to boot. Let's just hope its connectivity holds up long-term, because there is no USB connectivity whatsoever.
For
- Top-tier build quality
- Ultra-wideband (UWB) connection
- Hot-swappable batteries
- Lightweight
- Web software
- Optical clicks feel and sound great
Against
- Expensive
- No port for a cable at all
- Not the most defined scroll wheel feel
PC Gamer's got your back
This has been quite the year for competitive/esports gaming mice. First we had the Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike (and now the improved X3), then the Razer Viper V4 Pro. Now, with this Rival Pro, we have SteelSeries finally rejoining the former brands in the sphere of top-tier competitive gaming mice. A true return to form, in my humble opinion.
What makes for a good competitive gaming mouse? Well, it's often said that 'shape is king', so a comfy shape is certainly an important factor. In addition, you want it to be lightweight, which means no heavier than about 60 g and preferably a fair bit lighter than this. You also, of course, want flawless connectivity, an accurate and reliable sensor, and solid build quality.
As far as I'm concerned, if all those are implemented correctly, then that's everything you need to land in top-tier territory. But mice can also offer some nice-to-haves such as 8K polling and the ability to adjust things, such as lift-off distance (LOD) or sensor frame rate. They might also have completely new technologies, which is where the Superstrike gets its claim to competitive fame thanks to its inductive technology and rapid trigger clicks.
Buy if...
✅ You want the comfiest palm grip: If you like an ergonomic slant to your mouse for a comfy palm grip, alongside the Zowie EC2-DW, the SteelSeries Rival Pro is the best I've tried. The difference being here you're also getting a lighter and more premium-feeling mouse.
Don't buy if...
❌ You want something tried and tested: There are some new technologies here (UWB, mixed polling, 'true' 8K) which should, in theory, be better than the norm. However we can't know yet whether they will cause any issues over the long-term given the complete lack of a cable for installing firmware updates, for instance.
This SteelSeries mouse doesn't have anything quite as fancy as haptic-inductive clicks, but that doesn't bar it from being a great competitive mouse, just as surely as it doesn't bar the current best gaming mouse on the market, the Viper V4 Pro, from the same accolade. When it comes to all the other areas that make for a great competitive gaming mouse, the Rival Pro is up there with the best of them and is superb for gamers who use a palm grip. And it even has a couple of its own tricks up its sleeve.
The first trick is its 'Infinite Power System', ie, hot-swappable batteries. They're designed well and once you've swapped them a few times to get used to it, you can flip the mouse over and replace it with the backup in the wireless receiver/charger very easily. There's no additional battery inside the mouse itself, so the connection will cut out when you swap, but I've had no problems at all with the mouse turning back on and connecting straight away before it hits the pad again.
It's necessary that this system work smoothly because SteelSeries has decided to completely remove the option to connect the mouse to your PC with a cable. It's fully wireless with no USB-C port, which is a bold decision, but I'm sure eliminating the internals for a cable also helps keep the mouse light despite its hot-swappable battery system.
In addition to the batteries, another thing that will presumably help ensure the lack of a cable isn't too much of an issue is that SteelSeries is opting for an ultra-wideband (UWB) rather than a 2.4 GHz connection. This means more bandwidth and less channel interference from other devices, which should, in theory, make for a more reliable connection, and I must say I've had zero issues with the mouse remaining connected and stable after my initial setup. We've seen whispers of other, lesser-known brands opting for UWB connectivity, but it's still very new and niche.

I naturally feel (as I think others might) a little wary of completely ditching a wired connection. But I suppose that's how many PC gamers felt when mice started going wireless in general, even with the option for a cable. And I must admit, after everything was set up the way I wanted it, my experience with this mouse's UWB connectivity and battery system has been flawless. Perhaps SteelSeries will herald in a new era that sees us cut the cord fully, and eventually we won't worry about it.
It definitely feels worth it to keep the weight low, and here we come to the nuts and bolts: shape, weight, and build quality. The long and short of it is that this is, I think, the most comfortable I've ever felt with a mouse under my hand as a palm gripper.
Previously, my go-to mouse was the Zowie EC2-DW, which shares a similar ergonomic shape that's designed for palm grip. Comparing the two, the SteelSeries Rival Pro has a slightly less pronounced left-side slope, leaving me to feel my hand is resting a little flatter than with the Zowie. But it's still curved and ergonomic, and the curves feel, well, curvy, rather than sharp. The whole thing is helped by a nice matte texture to the surface that feels fantastic under the hand.
I'm not actually sure whether I prefer the shape of the Zowie or the Rival Pro; they both feel very similarly ergonomic and well-suited to a full palm grip for low-sensitivity gameplay in tactical shooters. It's a close call but the SteelSeries mouse is now my go-to, primarily because I prefer its matte coating and because it has the hot-swappable battery system. And because it's lighter.
Build quality is fantastic, too. The buttons (including side buttons) feel sturdy and responsive and don't have a hint of pre- or post-travel to them, and try as I might I cannot get a creak out of this thing when I squeeze it. What's especially impressive is that the left and right mouse buttons are optical ones but they feel and sound mechanical rather than loud or hollow which can often happen with optical switches—SteelSeries says it worked closely with the switch manufacturer to achieve this.
The only problem I have is the scroll wheel action isn't as defined and satisfying as some others—the steps are more defined on the Viper V4 Pro and Superstrike, for instance. Still, it's far from the worst scroll wheel I've felt, and everything else about the mouse feels lovely.
